questions.q: Why can't a Raspberry Pi read a smoothly-varying analog sensor directly?
choices: Its GPIO pins are too slow to keep up with analog signals
It has no ADC (Analogue-to-Digital Converter) — every GPIO pin is purely digital, reading only HIGH or LOW
Analog sensors need 5 V, which the Pi cannot supply
The gpiozero library refuses to read analog values
questions.explain: Unlike an Arduino, the Pi has no built-in ADC, so its GPIO pins can only distinguish HIGH from LOW. To read a true analog voltage you must add an external ADC such as the MCP3008, or use a sensor that gives a digital output.

questions.q: For a Pi plant monitor, why is a capacitive soil sensor with a digital output a good choice?
choices: It is the only sensor that works at 5 V
Its digital wet/dry output needs no ADC, and capacitive probes don't corrode in the soil
It measures temperature as well as moisture
It connects over SPI and is faster than other sensors
questions.explain: A capacitive sensor's onboard chip gives a clean digital HIGH/LOW the Pi can read directly with no ADC, and capacitive probes avoid the corrosion that plagues current-passing resistive sensors.

questions.q: Which DHT22 approach actually works on a Raspberry Pi 5 running Bookworm?
choices: The legacy Adafruit_DHT library installed with pip
The pigpio daemon (pigpiod) with its DHT helper
The current adafruit_dht library together with adafruit-blinka, catching occasional checksum errors
RPi.GPIO with a manual timing loop
questions.explain: On the Pi 5, the archived Adafruit_DHT and the pigpio daemon both fail. The working combination is adafruit-circuitpython-dht plus a recent adafruit-blinka (which routes through lgpio), with a retry to handle the DHT22's occasional checksum RuntimeError.

questions.q: Which file mode should a data logger use so that new readings are added without erasing the existing history?
choices: "w" (write)
"a" (append)
"r" (read)
"x" (exclusive)
questions.explain: Mode "w" erases the file first, and "r" only reads. Append mode "a" adds each new row to the end of the file while keeping everything already logged — exactly what a logger needs.

questions.q: After logging readings to a CSV, what is a clean way to find the warmest temperature of the day?
choices: Open the file in "w" mode and overwrite it with the maximum
Read the rows back with csv.DictReader into a list of dictionaries, pull the temperatures into a list, and use max()
It is impossible once data is written to a file
Use a voltage divider to scale the readings
questions.explain: Reading the CSV back with csv.DictReader gives a list of dictionaries; a list comprehension extracts the temperature values, and Python's built-in max() (and min()) finds the extremes. This is the standard 'read data back to find min/max' pattern.
